newsitem.title: LEBANON: Hizbollah makes comeback in Lebanon election.
newsitem.headline: Hizbollah makes comeback in Lebanon election.

text.p: The pro-Iranian Hizbollah made a political comeback in the fourth round of Lebanon's general election, winning the four seats it contested after losing two in earlier rounds of voting.

Hizbollah's (Party of God's) candidates won in south Lebanon under a Syrian-sponsored alliance with the secular Shi'ite Moslem movement Amal which also won five seats in the 128-member house, according to partial results issued on Monday.
Final results are expected on Tuesday, officials said.

The joint ticket, forged at the last minute under Syrian mediation, swept all 23 southern seats in parliament. It included four government ministers and Bahia Hariri, sister of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.
Well-known opposition candidates like Elias Abou Rizk, outspoken head of Lebanon's labour confederation, and Marxist deputy Habib Saadeq, lost despite winning a lot of votes.

Despite the success of the joint ticket, political analysts doubted the Hizbollah-Amal deal would translate into an alliance in the new parliament. The two groups are rivals for leadership of Lebanon's 1.3 million Shi'ite Moslem community and fought a sporadic war in the late 1980s.
"Agreements made now are not going to hold. Things will get back to normal in a few weeks time and when the chips are down they will go their separate ways," an analyst said.
That also applied to an election alliance between Hariri and Nabih Berri, the Amal chief and speaker of parliament who won re-election on Sunday, the analyst said.
Hariri and Berri fought non-stop for supremacy in the previous parliament but have united during the election to keep opposition figures out of the new parliament.

However, Hizbollah's success ended speculation that Syria, which has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and a powerful say in its affairs, had decided it was time to cut the fundamentalist movement down to size and reduce its strength in parliament.

Sharp attacks on Hizbollah during the campaign by Hariri had raised expectations that Syria wanted to curb the group. Hariri said the election was a contest between moderates and extremists and criticised Hizbollah's policies and aims.
The speculation intensified when candidates of the pro-Syrian government defeated two Hizbollah deputies who ran for re-election in Mount Lebanon and Beirut.

Beirut newspapers then said Syria appeared to be sending a message to the United States and Israel that it was able to rein in Hizbollah, whose guerrillas are fighting Israeli troops occupying a south Lebanon border strip, at will.
But the last-minute deal in the south actually increased Hizbollah's deputies from the south from two to four and showed that Syria still needed Hizbollah in its battle with Israel, analysts said.

It also included Amal-Hizbollah cooperation in the final round of voting next Sunday in the eastern Bekaa Valley where they have formed a joint list including three Hizbollah candidates and two supporters.
That will leave Hizbollah with a total of seven deputies and two supporters in the new parliament compared with eight deputies and four supporters in the outgoing chamber.
"I don't think Syria would think of weakening Hizbollah in the south," an analyst said.

The Lebanese Association for Democracy of Elections said the vote was marred by many of the abuses it noted during earlier rounds including massive omissions from voters lists, illegal presence of police inside polling stations, reports of bribery and fraudulent voting on behalf of dead or emigre voters.
